learn.title: be supposed to: present and future
learn.html:
be supposed to has several meanings depending on the context. It is formed with be (am / is / are) + supposed + to + base verb. The -d at the end of supposed is required.

MeaningExample
'They say that…' (what is expected or said)It's supposed to be a barbecue. (= They say it's a barbecue.)
'I have to…' (obligation, like have to)I'm supposed to work tomorrow. (= I have to work tomorrow.)
'I shouldn't…' (like should not)He's not supposed to eat chocolate. (= He shouldn't eat chocolate.)
Contrast with realityI'm supposed to be studying for an exam (but I'm not).
  • Negative: isn't / aren't / am not supposed to.
  • Question: Are we supposed to dress up?
  • It is used a lot to talk about rules, expectations and rumors.

watch.why: The be and the -d are missing: am supposed to.

watch.wrong: He's not suppose to eat chocolate.
watch.right: He's not supposed to eat chocolate.
watch.why: It is a past participle: supposed, with -d.

watch.wrong: She's supposed go to the party.
watch.right: She's supposed to go to the party.
watch.why: The to is missing between supposed and the verb.
After supposed to comes the base form of the verb.

learn.title: was / were supposed to and was / were going to
learn.html:
In the past, was / were supposed to expresses what was expected to happen but did not happen (or will not happen): They were supposed to come at 7:00 (but they didn't). / I wasn't supposed to go by myself (but I'll have to).

was / were going to has a similar use: plans that did not happen, or a past intention.

FormExampleMeaning
was / were supposed to + baseShe was supposed to call me.It was expected, but she didn't call.
wasn't / weren't supposed to + baseI wasn't supposed to tell anyone.It was forbidden, or I shouldn't have.
was / were going to + baseHe was going to give us directions (but he didn't).A plan or intention that did not happen.
wasn't going to + baseI wasn't going to go (but I guess I will).I wasn't planning to go, but I changed my mind.
  • Question: Weren't you supposed to get off work early? (with a tone of surprise)
  • Notice the verb after to: always the base form, never the past.

watch.wrong: She was supposed to came at six.
watch.right: She was supposed to come at six.
watch.why: After to comes the base form, even though the sentence is in the past.

watch.wrong: He was going to gave us directions.
watch.right: He was going to give us directions.

watch.wrong: Did you suppose to bring the cake?
watch.right: Were you supposed to bring the cake?
watch.why: It uses be (was / were), not did, and supposed with -d.

watch.wrong: I was suppose to call him.
watch.right: I was supposed to call him.

learn.title: Inseparable phrasal verbs with get
learn.html:
Inseparable phrasal verbs do not allow the object to go between the verb and the particle. The object goes after the particle or preposition, and it can be a noun, a verb with -ing or a pronoun:

StructureExample
verb + particle + objectWeren't you supposed to get off work early? / She'll never get over feeling embarrassed. / I'm sure she'll get over it.
verb + particle + preposition + objectA: Can I get away with wearing pants? B: No. You can't get away with it.
A: Couldn't you get out of the meeting? B: No, I couldn't get out of it.
A: Did you get around to buying a gift? B: No, I never got around to it.
  • With a pronoun, the pronoun goes at the end: get over it, NOT get it over.
  • The prepositions to, with, of are part of the verb: get around to, get away with, get out of.
  • After the preposition, a verb takes -ing: get around to buying.

watch.wrong: I never got around buying a gift.
watch.right: I never got around to buying a gift.
watch.why: The preposition to is missing: get around to + -ing.

watch.right: He can't get away with it.

watch.wrong: Could you get out the meeting?
watch.right: Could you get out of the meeting?
watch.why: Of is needed: get out of.
Inseparable: the object goes after the particle.

learn.title: Strategy: checking your understanding (statement questions and so)
learn.html:
In real conversation you can ask questions in the form of a statement, with rising intonation, to confirm what you understood. They often end in huh or right.

  • A: I just don't like big groups of people. B: So you're not going to go? (more natural than So aren't you going to go?)
  • So parties aren't your thing, huh? / You're going this time, right?

So is used for several things:

  • Starting a topic: So, there's another work party on Friday, right?
  • Checking that you understood: So parties aren't your thing, huh?
  • Leaving the idea open for the other person to conclude: I'd rather talk one on one, so …
  • Closing a topic or a story: So yeah, I'll just say I have other plans.

learn.title: The uses of as: because, being, while
learn.html:
The word as connects ideas and has three meanings. It is very useful in intermediate-to-advanced written texts.

as = …Example
beingAs an extrovert, I love to socialize. (= Being an extrovert, …)
becauseI enjoy going out to new places as I love to meet new people.
while / whenI get excited as the weekend gets closer.
  • As + noun talks about your role or identity: As a teacher, As an introvert.
  • Don't use like in that case: Like an introvert means 'similar to an introvert'.
  • With the meaning 'while', describe two things that change or happen at the same time.

watch.right: As an extrovert, I love parties.

watch.wrong: Like an introvert, I need quiet time to recharge.
watch.right: As an introvert, I need quiet time to recharge.

watch.wrong: I stayed home as of I was tired.
watch.right: I stayed home as I was tired.
watch.why: As + subject + verb; it does not take of.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• All I know is that … — 'the only thing I know is that…'.
  • I don't get it. — 'I don't understand it.'
  • Oh, come on! — used to insist or to show you don't believe something.
  • By the way, … — 'by the way…', to change the topic.
  • Anyway, … — 'anyway…', to return to a topic or to close it.
  • I'm looking forward to … — 'I can't wait to…'.
  • It's supposed to be … — 'it is meant to be…'.
  • I was going to … but … — 'I was going to… but…'.

write.prompt: A friend invited you to an event (a wedding, a barbecue, a surprise party) but you can't or don't want to go. Write an email of 180 to 250 words: thank them, explain what you were going to do and what you were supposed to do, what you tried in order to get out of it, and suggest an alternative plan. Use be supposed to, was / were going to and at least two phrasal verbs with get. Example opening: Hi Pablo, thanks so much for inviting me to the barbecue. I was going to come, but …
targets: be supposed to / was supposed to
checklist: Between 180 and 250 words
At least one sentence with am / is / are supposed to
At least one with was / were supposed to and one with was / were going to
Base verb after supposed to and going to
Two phrasal verbs with get (get out of, get around to…) with the object well placed
One sentence with as (because, being or while)
Email greeting and sign-off
write.model:
Hi Pablo,

Thanks so much for inviting me to the barbecue. I was going to come, but something unexpected has happened. I'm supposed to finish a report by Monday, and I haven't even started it. My boss is supposed to read it first thing in the morning, so I can't leave it for later.

I was supposed to work on it last week, but I never got around to it. Honestly, I tried to get out of it by asking a colleague to take over, but she was going to travel this weekend, so it didn't work. I also thought about asking for an extension. I was going to talk to my boss yesterday, but he was in meetings all day. In the end I had to get on with it by myself.

As I won't be able to finish before Sunday night, I really can't join you. I feel terrible, because I was looking forward to seeing everyone, and I'm sure it will be a great party. I hope you aren't upset.

How about this: next Saturday I could invite you and a few friends to my place? I'm going to make my famous tacos al pastor. We could watch the football match and catch up. Let me know if that works.

Have a great barbecue, and say hi to everyone from me!

Best wishes,
Daniel

At least 5 expressions from the social vocabulary

write.model:
As an introvert, I like parties, but only for a short time. I'm somewhere between an extrovert and an introvert: being in a small group makes me feel relaxed, while big crowds make me tired.

When I arrive at a party, I usually look for a quiet corner. As I'm not very good at small talk, I often stand next to the food and wait for someone to start a conversation. Once I get to know people, I feel more comfortable. I have to get used to the noise first, and then I can enjoy myself. My friends, who are more outgoing, always make me laugh, and I like being a good listener while they tell their stories.

Last week there was a birthday party, and this is what happened:

"So you're not staying for the cake, right?"
"I'm afraid not. I have an early day tomorrow."
"You always do, huh?"

As I enjoy deep conversations more than dancing, I usually leave early. As I walk home, I feel happy and calm. By the way, I'm not shy at work; it is just that big events are exhausting.

Anyway, all I know is that I need time alone to recharge. It doesn't mean I don't like people. It just means that I need a balance between going out and staying home, and I'm happy with that.

reading.title: The party I couldn't get out of
reading.intro: Read the story of an introverted person and answer the questions.
paragraphs: I'm not a party person. As an introvert, I recharge by spending time alone, and my idea of a perfect Friday night involves a sofa, a blanket, and a good series. So when my co-worker Daniela announced a surprise party for our boss, my heart sank. I could already imagine the music, the crowd, and the endless questions about my weekend plans.

"You're coming, right?" she asked at the coffee machine. I smiled, the way you do when you would prefer to disappear. The party was supposed to be small, just the team, but I got the feeling that it would turn into one of those loud evenings where you have to engage in chitchat for hours. I was going to say that I had other plans. In fact, I had already prepared a little white lie about a sick cousin. But Daniela looked so excited that I couldn't get out of it.

On Saturday I was supposed to arrive at seven, and I tried to get ready at the last minute so that I wouldn't have to wait around. Naturally, I got lost, and I walked in twenty minutes late, feeling every eye in the room turn toward me. The living room was full of people holding paper plates. I looked for a quiet corner, hoping to keep a low profile, but my boss, who is a real social animal, found me immediately. "So parties aren't your thing, huh?" he said, smiling. I laughed. "To be honest, no."

Then something unexpected happened. Instead of pushing me into the center of attention, he told me he wasn't a big fan of large groups either. As an ambitious young manager, he had learned to be good at small talk, but it had taken years, and he still felt exhausted afterwards. We talked one on one for twenty minutes, and for the first time in months I felt that someone at work really understood me.

I stayed for three hours, which is a personal record. I didn't get around to dancing, of course, but I helped with the cake and listened to a colleague's travel stories. On the way home, I realized that I had spent weeks dreading that party, and it had been fine. I won't say I'm a new person; I'm still going to choose the sofa most Fridays. But next time someone asks, "You're coming, right?", I might say yes without looking for an excuse. As the saying goes, the hardest part is getting out of the house.

tasks.prompt: Tell about a plan that did not happen: something you were going to do or were supposed to do, but didn't. Explain why.
questions: What were you supposed to do last weekend?
Was there something you were going to do but didn't?
What are you supposed to do tomorrow?
tasks.model: Last weekend I was supposed to visit my grandmother, but I got sick. I was going to take her a cake, but I never got around to buying the ingredients. Tomorrow I'm supposed to work until five, and then I'm going to call her. I'm really looking forward to seeing her.
checklist: was / were supposed to + base verb
was / were going to + base verb
get around to + -ing
look forward to

tasks.prompt: Talk about your social style: whether you are an extrovert or an introvert, how you feel at parties and why.
questions: Are you an extrovert or an introvert?
Are you good at small talk?
Do you like being the center of attention?
How do you usually celebrate your birthday?
tasks.model: As an introvert, I prefer small groups. I'm not very good at small talk, so I usually talk one on one. I don't like being the center of attention; I keep a low profile at parties. For my birthday, I have dinner with three or four close friends.
checklist: As + identity
Social vocabulary from the unit
be good at + noun / -ing
'an' before a vowel sound

tasks.prompt: A coworker invites you to a party, but you don't want to go. Make up an excuse or try to get out of it, and confirm what you understood with statement questions.
questions: Are you coming to the party on Friday?
Can't you get out of your plans?
So you're not going to go?
What are you going to say to your friend?
tasks.model: I'm sorry, I can't make it. I was going to come, but I'm supposed to work on Saturday morning. So you really want me there, right? To be honest, I'm not a party person, but I'll try to get there for an hour. I'm looking forward to the cake!
checklist: was going to / am supposed to
get out of / get around to
statement question with right or huh
To be honest / By the way

repeat: It's supposed to be a surprise party.
I was supposed to arrive at seven.
He was going to give us directions.
I never got around to buying a gift.
So parties aren't your thing, huh?
As an extrovert, I love to socialize.
